transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-21 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Sofia (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Maya (BlueHarbor CTO), Ethan (ML Eng), Rosa (SRE)

[00:00] Sofia: Hey everybody thanks for joining, um let's do quick intros then jump into the TTFT vs TPOT question. Diego and I will drive the technical + commercial pieces.
[00:14] Maya: hi all, Maya here, quick context: BlueHarbor runs an analytics assistant that serves summary prompts and some long-form generation, high variance in token lengths, we care about 95th and 99th percentiles, cost is material.
[00:28] Diego: cool, that's helpful. Ethan, can you call out typical prompt lengths and response sizes?
[00:33] Ethan: yeah so median prompt ~120 tokens, replies vary — med reply 80 tokens, tail up to 2k tokens for long summaries; 10% of calls are >1k. Also we have a short latency-sensitive path for interactive UI where first token matters a lot.
[00:47] Sofia: that maps cleanly to TTFT (first-token latency) for the interactive path and TPOT for the batch/long generation, right. Today tell us what y'all measure and what SLOs you'd expect?
[01:05] Maya: we currently blink metrics from our old endpoint: p95 ~ 450ms for small prompts but p99 spikes to 1.8s, that's unacceptable for the editor flow. For long jobs we care more about throughput and dollars per 1M tokens.
[01:20] Diego: okay, so two axes: immediate first-byte latency and total completion time per request. For framing — we're proposing p95 TTFT target of 200-300ms on the editor flow, p99 under 600ms when running on a dedicated pool; TPOT p95 depends on length, we often express it as per-token ms plus fixed overhead. We'll want to benchmark both.
[01:44] Rosa: quick infra note — for security we need VPC peering option for the pilot and audit logs. Also keep in mind our infra has bursty traffic during business hours.
[01:55] Sofia: we'll include Dedicated and Private options in the pilot plan — Diego can you outline the measurement plan?
[02:04] Diego: yes. Step one: customer supplies a 24–72h anonymized traffic sample and the top prompt templates. We'll create traffic tiles: interactive (short), medium, long. For each tile we run three experiments: cold-start (KV cache empty), warm-start (typical warmed caches, simulate reuse), and steady-state at target QPS. Metrics: TTFT p50/p95/p99, TPOT p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, cost/token estimate. We'll also capture CPU/GPU utilization and queue lengths.
[02:36] Ethan: how do you simulate KV cache warm? Our cache pattern is 60% of calls share prefixes.
[02:42] Diego: we replay sequences that preserve prefix reuse and include warmup runs before measurement intervals. There's some approximation of user sessions; we ask you to flag any synthetic-only templates.
[02:51] Maya: what about batching? we can't change client behavior easily for the editor flow; for long jobs we can allow batching in the request layer.
[03:00] Diego: batching will be part of the sweep matrix. We'll test continuous batching at several batch sizes and dynamic batching latency SLOs. For the editor path, batching often hurts TTFT because it adds queuing, so we'll measure with batching disabled and with micro-batches.
[03:14] Sofia: and quantization/weights — do we test int8 or higher?
[03:18] Diego: yes, matrix: float16 baseline, int8 quantized (if model supports it), and a mixed-precision profile. We'll report quality regressions by running a small eval set of prompts you provide. You flagged quality sensitivity?
[03:33] Maya: yes for clinical summarization quality matters — need thresholds. We'll give an eval set.
[03:38] Rosa: timeline: how long for the lab sweeps and the pilot?
[03:42] Diego: lab sweeps (benchmark runs) typically 2–3 days to run full matrix on 1–2 hardware shapes, analysis 2 days. Pilot — we suggested a 48–72 hour pilot with your traffic replayed into a dedicated pool to validate end-to-end behavior and operational integration.
[03:58] Sofia: cost question from our side: what will customer see as unit economics?
[04:02] Diego: we'll compute cost per 1M tokens and cost per peak-QPS-hour using the Dedicated pool pricing. We'll include burst and fallback scenarios.
[04:11] Ethan: about SLOs — do you recommend strict p99 targets or weighted metrics? Our user experience tolerates a small tail for long generations.
[04:19] Diego: recommended approach: set TTFT hard SLOs for interactive flows (p95 and p99 targets) and use weighted TPOT SLOs for long jobs — e.g., p95 completion under X ms for short+medium, and p99 under Y ms for long but with a higher tolerance. Also include a cost-performance guardrail; acceptance requires both latency and cost thresholds.
[04:44] Maya: can you give concrete numbers for pilot acceptance?
[04:47] Sofia: proposed acceptance criteria (draft): interactive TTFT p95 <= 250ms, p99 <= 600ms; long generation TPOT p95 <= 2.5s for <=512-token outputs, p99 <= 5s for <=2k outputs, cost per 1M tokens within 20% of the current baseline. Also no functional quality regression on the eval set >1.5% drop.
[05:10] Ethan: the cost part is tricky; our current baseline is messy. We'll supply approximate spend.
[05:15] Diego: that's fine — we'll show relative improvements and absolute estimates.
[05:20] Rosa: security items again — audit logs retention and SSO.
[05:23] Sofia: we'll attach the security pack and SOC 2 summary.
[05:26] Diego: measurement nuances: clock sync is important for p99 across distributed workers, so we'll run everything against the Redwood lab harness with unified timestamps, and we'll add synthetic latency markers.
[05:37] Maya: what about client-side rendering time? sometimes first token arrives but the UI processing adds 80–120ms.
[05:42] Diego: good point, we'll provide TTFT server-side and also an optional synthetic end-to-end metric that includes a simulated client processing delay; we'll label both.
[05:52] Sofia: do we need to worry about model variants? you mentioned fallback to smaller models under load.
[05:57] Diego: yes, part of the routing policy test: baseline model (preferred), fallback model (smaller) and what that does to SLOs and quality. We'll run canary scenarios and verify graceful degradation.
[06:09] Ethan: how will you report variance? a single p99 can hide step-changes.
[06:14] Diego: we'll report time series with sliding-window percentiles and include a risk register noting any patterns (e.g., periodic queue spikes at XX minute mark).
[06:24] Maya: are there any observability hooks we need to add? traces?
[06:27] Diego: yes please enable request IDs and sample traces; Redwood will ingest traces for correlated debugging. We'll provide trace sampling instrumentation.
[06:36] Sofia: next up — schedule. We aim to start lab runs next Tue after you share traffic. Pilot the week after if lab looks good. That fit?
[06:42] Maya: yes that works for us. We have a compliance window at month-end but pilot before that is fine.
[06:48] Diego: one more note on sampling: for p99 accuracy you need large samples; we'll recommend at least 100k requests per tile or synthetic extrapolation if not feasible. We'll explain confidence intervals in the report.
[06:59] Rosa: ok, and we'll need RBAC for our team in the console during the pilot.
[07:03] Sofia: we'll set that up; Diego will coordinate.
[07:08] Maya: great, thanks — any other questions?
[07:11] Sofia: last bullet — we'll include a small spreadsheet that maps traffic tiles to SLOs and pass/fail criteria. Diego will own the benchmark run book.
[07:20] Diego: yep I'll share the run book and a template for the traffic sample.
[07:25] Sofia: perfect. Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the artifacts and schedule the lab run.
[07:29] Maya: thanks all.
